Hallucination and confabulation

Whether the fluent wrong answer is a defect awaiting a patch or a property of the mechanism — and what changes in a product organisation once you decide which.

OneTwo rooms, one week apart

On the evening of 3 September 2026, Kavya Iyer sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of an office block off Bellandur, Bengaluru, looking at a clause her sales head had already verbally agreed to. Kavya was Director of Product at Prashna Support Cloud, a nine-year-old company selling an AI support agent to Indian enterprises: sixty clients, ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, and one account — a large non-banking financial company with a retail lending book — that alone contributed ₹11 crore. The NBFC's renewal, due 30 September, carried a new service level. The agent's answers to customer questions about loan terms, foreclosure charges and EMI schedules were to be "materially incorrect" in no more than 0.1% of cases, verified quarterly by the client's own audit team, with a service credit of ₹40 lakh per quarter for breach.

Prashna's own measurement of that agent, on a hand-labelled set of 900 questions, was 1.8%. Devendra Rao, the sales head, was in Edison, New Jersey, and had written in the deal thread that the number would "come down with the next model anyway". Kavya's engineering lead, Prateek Joshi in Pune, had replied at 2:40 a.m. India time with a single line: it will come down. It will not come down to zero, and 0.1% is a promise about the tail, not the average. Kavya had eleven working days to decide what Prashna would sign.

Six days later and 980 kilometres away, in Lower Parel, Mumbai, Aparna Sundaram was looking at a launch date. She ran product at Vivran Health, a consumer health app with 4.1 million monthly active users, sixty-two per cent of them in tier-two and tier-three towns, monetised through diagnostics bookings and a pharmacy tie-up. The growth team wanted "Ask about your medicine" live before Diwali on 8 November 2026, because the festival fortnight reliably produced the year's highest install volume. The feature would let a user photograph a prescription or type a brand name and ask questions: what is this for, can I take it with my blood pressure tablet, is there a cheaper generic.

Aparna's data scientist, Nikhil Bhagat in Toronto, had run 1,200 real user questions through the candidate system and produced a number she could not unsee: on questions about drug interactions, 6.3% of answers contained a statement that was not supported by the reference formulary and, in nineteen cases, was actively wrong about a dosage. Her designer, Lena Krüger in Berlin, wanted the answer surface redesigned so that the model's prose was subordinate to a scanned leaflet. Her growth lead wanted the prose, because the prose was what tested well. India's Drugs and Cosmetics rules, the CDSCO framework and the DPDP Act all sat in the background, none of them written with a generative assistant in mind.

Kavya and Aparna were facing the same question from opposite ends of the market, and it is the question this topic exists to answer: is the confidently invented sentence a bug that will be fixed, or a permanent property of the machinery that a product must be built around?

TwoThe idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

Begin with a definition precise enough to be measured. A hallucination is a statement produced by a generative model that is asserted in the same register as its supported statements but has no basis in the input provided to the model or in the world. The literature since about 2022 splits this into two kinds, and the split is operationally important. An intrinsic hallucination contradicts the source material supplied to the model — the document says thirty days, the answer says sixty. An extrinsic hallucination adds content the source neither supports nor contradicts — a clause, a citation, a side effect, an interest rate that simply is not in the corpus. Intrinsic errors are cheap to detect mechanically because there is something to compare against. Extrinsic errors are the expensive ones, and they are the majority.

The word arrived from computer vision and machine translation. Image-captioning researchers used it around 2018 for systems that described objects absent from the photograph; neural translation researchers used it for fluent target sentences unrelated to the source. Surveys of the phenomenon in natural language generation consolidated the intrinsic/extrinsic vocabulary in 2022, and the term went mainstream when conversational models reached the public.

Almost immediately there was an objection to the word, and the objection is the intellectual core of the topic. Confabulation, the alternative, comes from clinical neuropsychology: patients with certain amnesic syndromes, described from Sergei Korsakoff's work in the late 1880s onward, fill gaps with coherent, sincere, plausible narrative and show no awareness that anything has been filled in. Hallucination implies a perceptual apparatus misfiring. Confabulation implies a generative apparatus doing precisely what it does, over a gap. The second is the better analogy, because in a language model nothing misfires. The mechanism that produces the true answer and the mechanism that produces the invented clause are not merely similar; they are the same mechanism running on the same weights with the same objective.

Four schools now argue about what follows from that, and a product manager who can state each position in its own terms will be able to referee most disagreements between competent practitioners.

Positions are summarised for teaching. Individual researchers hold combinations; the engineering-defect and incentive schools in particular overlap heavily in practice.

The practical synthesis that nobody quite holds — and which is worth naming so it can be avoided — is that everyone agrees the rate falls and disagrees only about the limit. That is not right. The schools disagree about what a product team should do. The engineering-defect school implies investment in models and patience. The structural school implies investment in grounding, abstention and workflow. The incentive school implies investment in internal evaluation design. The epistemic school implies investment in interface: never present generated prose in a register that invites belief.

ThreeMechanics in depth, with the numbers worked

A language model assigns a probability distribution over the next token — a word fragment of roughly three-quarters of a word — given the sequence so far, and is trained by minimising cross-entropy against human text. Two consequences follow that experts treat as obvious and newcomers rarely see stated.

The first is that fluency and truth are produced by the same computation. There is no branch in the network where the model consults a store of facts and, failing to find one, takes a different path. Whatever continuation is most probable is what emerges. When Prashna's agent is asked about foreclosure charges on a loan product it has never seen documentation for, the most probable continuation is a well-formed sentence containing a plausible percentage, because that is what such sentences contain.

The second is calibration. A model trained to match a distribution will, if it succeeds, reproduce the uncertainty in that distribution — it will be right about as often as it "should" be. This is the hinge of the structural argument. Suppose the corpus contains 118,000 discrete facts about a client's product lines, and 31% of them appear exactly once. Facts that appear once give the model almost nothing to generalise from; from the model's perspective they are arbitrary. A generator calibrated to that distribution cannot reliably distinguish an arbitrary fact it has seen from one it has not, and so on questions drawn from that singleton stratum it will err at a rate in the same neighbourhood as the singleton rate itself. The bound is a statement about calibrated generators answering from parametric memory. It is not a statement about a system that looks the fact up — which is exactly why grounding is the correct response to it rather than a workaround.

The incentive arithmetic, in three lines

Consider a benchmark that awards 1 for a correct answer, 0 for a wrong one and 0 for "I don't know". A model that estimates a 40% chance of being right scores an expected 0.40 by guessing and exactly 0 by abstaining. Guessing dominates, and any training process that optimises against such benchmarks will select for guessing. Now introduce a penalty k for a wrong answer. Expected score from guessing is p − k(1 − p), which exceeds zero only when p > k/(1 + k). At k = 1 the model should guess only above 50% confidence; at k = 3, only above 75%; at k = 9, only above 90%. Prashna's internal eval scored abstention at zero for three years. Kavya had, without knowing it, been paying a team to optimise for confident guessing.

The retrieval decomposition

Grounding is best understood as a decomposition rather than a fix. Write the overall unsupported rate as the sum of two paths: retrieval misses, times the probability the model fabricates given a miss; plus retrieval hits, times the probability it fabricates anyway. Prashna's September figures were a 12% miss rate, a 34% fabrication rate given a miss, and a 0.8% fabrication rate given a hit.

The verification arithmetic, which almost nobody does

Verification means running a second process over the generated answer — a verbatim span match against the retrieved text, a natural-language-inference model asking whether the source entails each sentence, or self-consistency, where the question is answered five times and semantic disagreement between the samples is treated as a warning sign. A 2024 paper in Nature formalised the last of these as semantic entropy and, notably, used the word confabulation rather than hallucination in its title. Whatever the detector, the arithmetic that matters is Bayesian and is usually skipped.

Take Prashna at the 2.0% operating point and a detector with 85% recall and a 4% false-positive rate, applied to 10,000 answers. Two hundred answers are genuinely unsupported; the detector catches 170 and misses 30. Of the 9,800 sound answers, 4% — 392 — are flagged anyway. The human review queue therefore contains 562 items of which 170 are real: a precision of 30.2%. At ₹18 per review, that is ₹10,116 per 10,000 answers, and at the NBFC's volume of 2.4 lakh conversations a month, ₹2.43 lakh a month in review cost. The residual reaching the customer is 30 in 10,000, or 0.30% — still three times the SLA.

The second-order effect is the one senior practitioners watch for. Push recall from 85% to 95% along the same detector curve and the false-positive rate rises to roughly 12%: the residual falls to 0.10%, exactly the SLA, but the queue swells to 1,366 items per 10,000 answers, review cost rises to about ₹5.9 lakh a month, and — this is the part that kills deployments — reviewer attention degrades. A queue that is 86% false alarms trains humans to approve without reading. The measured 70% human catch rate that everyone puts in the model is itself a function of queue precision, and it decays. Verification systems do not fail by missing things; they fail by crying wolf until nobody looks.

FourWhen the standard treatment applies, and when it misleads

The standard treatment — ground it, cite it, verify the citation, abstain when unsure, review the residual — rests on four claims that can be stated as tests and applied to a specific product.

Claim one: there exists a corpus that contains the answer. For Prashna this is true and checkable: the NBFC's product documentation, circulars and terms are finite, versioned and owned. For Vivran it is only partly true. Questions about what a molecule is for are answerable from a formulary. Questions of the form "can I take this with my blood pressure tablet" depend on the user's other medicines, their dose and their clinical history, none of which are in any corpus Vivran holds. Where the claim fails, grounding is not a partial fix; it is a false comfort, because a retrieval system will always return something and the returned text will make an unanswerable question look answered.

Claim two: support is decidable by a cheap process. True for Prashna, where a foreclosure charge is a number in a document. Weak for Vivran, where the supported statement and the unsupported one differ by a hedge.

Claim three: the cost of a wrong answer is bounded and recoverable. True for Prashna in the ordinary case — a customer told the wrong foreclosure charge is corrected by an agent, and the company can, if it chooses, honour the incorrect figure. False for Vivran in the interaction category, where the cost is not recoverable by refund.

Claim four: there is a human in a position to catch it. True for Prashna's escalation path. False for Vivran at 4.1 million users, where the human in the loop is the user, who is asking precisely because they do not know the answer.

Where the standard treatment is actively misleading is the case in which grounding raises apparent authority faster than it raises accuracy. Adding citations to Vivran's interaction answers would increase user trust measurably — Lena's prototype testing showed a nine-point lift in a stated-confidence question — while the underlying support was thin. That is a net worsening dressed as an improvement, and it is common enough to deserve a name in any product review.

FiveHard edge cases

Multi-product companies discover that the rate is not a company property. Prashna's agent ran across a support product, a knowledge-base authoring product and an outbound-messaging product, all sharing one model configuration. The measured rate differed by a factor of six between them, because the question distributions differed. A single company-wide number, reported to a board, is nearly always the average of things that should not be averaged.

Two-sided products have a structural blind spot. When a marketplace assistant invents a seller's return window, the buyer accepts the answer and the seller never learns it was given. The complaint arrives, if at all, as a dispute weeks later with no trace of the conversation. The only remedy is active sampling: audit a random slice of answers about the other side, because passive feedback will not arrive.

Regulated products raise a question of who is the speaker. If Vivran's assistant states a dosage, Indian pharmacy and drug regulation does not currently supply a tidy answer to whether that is information, advice or a claim. Mature companies in this position do not wait for the answer; they engineer the product so the question does not arise, by making the authoritative artefact — the manufacturer's leaflet, the doctor's prescription — the thing on screen and the generated text a navigational aid to it.

Hardware and software together creates a latency problem. Verification costs a second call and often a second model; on a device or in a voice channel where the user is waiting, the verification budget competes directly with responsiveness, and teams silently disable checks under load. The tell is a configuration flag with the word "fast" in it.

AI-native products face the compounding case. When one generated output becomes the input to the next — an agent that drafts a plan, then acts on its own plan — an unsupported statement in step two is treated as established fact by step five. The per-step rate looks acceptable and the per-task rate is catastrophic: at 2% per step, a nine-step chain has a 1 − 0.98⁹ ≈ 16.7% chance of carrying at least one fabrication.

At the organisational seams, the reality diverges from the stated process in a consistent way. Companies say they own the rate at the platform layer. What actually happens is that the platform team owns the model and the evaluation harness, application teams own the prompts and the corpora, and nobody owns the corpus's freshness. Mature companies handle it by making the index owner a named person with a service level on staleness, and by reporting the rate per application rather than per model.

SixNuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Faithfulness is not factuality

Two teams can measure diligently and disagree completely because one is asking whether the answer follows from the retrieved text and the other whether it is true. Both are legitimate; they diverge whenever the corpus is stale or wrong. The tell: a team that reports one number. Experts report both, and expect the gap between them to be the size of their documentation debt.

Abstention is a product decision priced in usage, not a safety setting

Every point of rate reduction is bought with refusals, and the exchange rate is steep near the bottom of the curve. The tell: a team that can quote its error rate but not its refusal rate has been optimising one number without watching its price.

Citations are generated unless something checks them

A clause number in an answer is more tokens. Prashna's audit found 11% of quoted spans absent from the cited document. The tell: users saying the citations "look right", which means they are checking plausibility rather than existence.

The rate is a property of the question distribution, not the model

Changing nothing but which users are onboarded changes the reported rate. The tell: a rate that moves after a sales push into a new segment, and an engineering team hunting for a regression that is not there.

Aggregate rates hide severity

An invented dosage and an invented office address are one event each in a spreadsheet. The tell: an eval with a single pass/fail column. Experts carry a severity taxonomy and weight by it, and are content to let the harmless rate rise if the severe rate falls.

Self-report is another generation

"Are you sure?" invokes the same mechanism and frequently flips correct answers under mild social pressure. Token-level probabilities and semantic disagreement across samples are real but weak signals. The tell: a confidence percentage rendered in the interface that was produced by asking the model for a confidence percentage.

Deeper retrieval trades one failure for another

More context reduces misses and introduces version confusion and distraction. The tell: an improvement in the headline rate accompanied by a fall in the refusal rate — the system did not get more accurate, it got more willing.

LLM-as-judge inherits the failure it is measuring

Using a model to grade a model is efficient and imports correlated blind spots, particularly a bias toward marking fluent answers correct. The tell: a judge whose agreement with human labels was measured once, at the start, on the easy half of the set.

The word "hallucination" is doing rhetorical work in the room

It suggests a rare, pathological event. Confabulation suggests a routine, expected output of a gap-filling process — which is what a board needs to hear before signing a contract. The tell: the phrase "edge case" attached to a 2% rate.

Zero is available and nobody wants it

A system that answers only from an exact-match lookup table has a rate of zero. Every intermediate design is a deliberate purchase of coverage with risk. The tell: an expert reframes "how do we eliminate hallucination" as "how much coverage are we buying, and at what price" within the first two minutes.

SevenAcross product types and company stages

In consumer products the binding constraint is reputational and categorical rather than statistical. Users tolerate a wrong restaurant recommendation and do not tolerate a wrong dosage; the design response is to refuse categories rather than to chase accuracy inside them. In B2B and enterprise the binding constraint is evidentiary: the buyer must be able to show a regulator or an auditor what the system said and what a human did about it, which makes citation verification and logging more valuable than a marginally better model. In platforms and marketplaces the constraint is the missing feedback loop described above. In hardware and physical goods the constraint is latency and offline operation, which pushes verification to the cloud and creates a degraded mode nobody tests. In AI-native products the constraint is compounding across steps.

Where the difference is often asserted and is not real: the underlying rate does not differ much by industry once question distribution is held constant, and "our domain is harder" is usually a statement about corpus quality rather than about language. Where stage genuinely matters: an early-stage company's most powerful lever is scope, because it can refuse eighty per cent of question types and still have a product, while a large company that has already sold generality must buy its way down with measurement, verification and workflow. A Series A company can ship a narrow assistant in six weeks; the same company at ₹500 crore of revenue needs a severity taxonomy, an index-freshness owner and a quarterly audit, and will take two quarters to change the same behaviour.

EightThree worked examples, including one that failed

Prashna: buying down a contractual number

Working from Table 2 and Figure 1, Kavya's team modelled the only combination that reached 0.10%: retrieval improvements to a 5% miss rate, abstention scoring changed so wrong answers were penalised at k = 3, and span verification on all quoted figures, giving a pre-detector rate of 1.26%; then a detector at 92% recall, leaving 0.10%. The cost was ₹1.9 crore of engineering over two quarters, a review queue of roughly ₹4.1 lakh a month, and a refusal rate rising from 5% to 13% — meaning the deflection rate the NBFC actually bought the product for would fall from 61% to about 54%, worth roughly ₹2.6 crore a year in the client's own agent costs. The SLA was reachable and it destroyed the business case for the product it was attached to.

Vivran: scoping instead of solving

Aparna's team split the feature into three question classes and measured separately. Identification questions — what is this molecule, what is it commonly prescribed for — were answerable from a licensed formulary at a 0.4% unsupported rate. Substitution questions — is there a cheaper generic — were answerable at 1.1% with a price feed. Interaction questions were answerable at 6.3% and unbounded in severity. Of 279,000 medicine questions a month, roughly 61% were identification, 22% substitution and 17% interaction. Shipping the first two classes and hard-refusing the third with a routed teleconsultation covered 83% of demand, and the refusal itself converted at 4.2% into a paid consultation — a business the free-text answer would have cannibalised.

Setubandh Freight Cloud: the failure and the recovery

A Chennai company selling a shipping-document assistant to exporters reported an unsupported rate of 0.6% for two quarters, measured with an LLM-as-judge pipeline. A customer audit in the Gulf found errors in bills of lading at a rate they estimated near 5%. The reconciliation, done on 400 hand-labelled answers, put the true rate at 4.9%: the judge had been prompted to check "whether the answer is consistent with the source", and it marked fluent, well-formatted answers consistent at a very high rate regardless of content. Judge-human agreement, measured for the first time, was 0.31 on the difficult stratum. The recovery took a quarter: a stratified human-labelled golden set of 700, a judge re-prompted to extract and check each claim separately, judge-human agreement re-measured monthly, and ₹1.7 crore of service credits negotiated with three clients. The lesson the team drew was not about judges. It was that they had never once asked what their measurement would look like if it were wrong.

TenWhere experts genuinely disagree

Steelman of the engineering-defect position. Measured rates on fixed benchmarks have fallen by large multiples across model generations without any change in product design; tool use converts many factual questions into lookups; verifier models are improving faster than generators on the narrow task of checking. The evidence is the trend line, and it is real. For this position to be wrong, the residual would have to be dominated by questions where no lookup exists and no verifier can adjudicate — which is precisely Vivran's interaction category, and precisely the stratum that grows as products get ambitious.

Steelman of the structural position. The calibration argument is a mathematical result, not a forecast: a generator faithful to a distribution inherits that distribution's arbitrariness. It explains why the same models that ace difficult reasoning benchmarks still invent citations, and why the tail resists. For it to be wrong in the way that matters commercially, deliberately miscalibrated models — trained to abstain far more often than a faithful generator would — would have to remain useful. That is an empirical question currently being answered, and the early answer is that users dislike abstention more than they dislike error.

Steelman of the incentive position. If benchmarks score abstention at zero, and post-training optimises against benchmarks, then confident guessing is a trained behaviour rather than an inherent one; the arithmetic in Section Three shows how sharp the incentive is. For it to be wrong, models trained with penalised guessing would have to fabricate at unchanged rates on retrieval-miss tails. Partial evidence exists on both sides; the honest position is that scoring reform moves behaviour substantially and does not remove the tail.

Steelman of the epistemic position. There is no assertion and no belief; the interface manufactures the impression of a claim by rendering tokens as prose in a chat bubble. This position predicts that the largest available risk reduction is in presentation, not in modelling — and the Vivran result, where the same underlying system was safe or dangerous depending on whether the leaflet or the prose was primary, is evidence for it. For it to be wrong, internal representations that track truth would have to be readable and actionable at deployment. Probing research suggests something is there; nothing yet suggests it is reliable enough to gate a product on.

ElevenWhat mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the topic uses the word correctly, knows that RAG helps, and asks engineering to reduce the rate. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways. They ask for the refusal rate in the same breath as the error rate, every time, so that no operating point is ever quoted as a single number. They insist on severity strata before they will look at an average, and they will trade a worse average for a better tail without hesitation. They treat measurement as the thing most likely to be broken — asking how the labels were made, what the judge agrees with humans about, and what the eval would look like if it were wrong — because the Setubandh failure is a measurement failure, not a model failure. And they change the workflow rather than the wording: no consequential action on a generated sentence alone, an authoritative artefact on screen wherever one exists, and a named owner for the freshness of every corpus the system reads.

TwelveWhat each protagonist decided

Kavya went back to the NBFC on 22 September and proposed replacing the single 0.1% figure with a three-tier commitment: 0.1% on a defined list of consequential question types — charges, rates, dates and eligibility — 1.5% on everything else, a published refusal rate that Prashna would not exceed, and a joint quarterly audit using a golden set the client's team would help build. Her reasoning was that a promise about the average was unmeasurable and a promise about the tail was purchasable; and that a service level she could hit at a refusal rate the client would hate was worse than no deal.

Aparna shipped identification and substitution on 22 October, ahead of Diwali, with the manufacturer's leaflet as the primary surface and generated prose confined to a summary strip above it, and hard-refused interaction questions with a routed teleconsultation. Her reasoning was that the interaction stratum failed all four tests in Section Four simultaneously — no corpus, no cheap decidability, unbounded cost, no human to catch it — and that no combination of prompting and grounding fixed a category that had no ground.

Three questions for discussion. First: Prashna can reach 0.1% and lose the business case for the product. Under what circumstances should a company sign a service level it can meet only by destroying the value it sells? Second: Vivran's refusal converted at 4.2% into paid consultations. How much of the apparent virtue of that decision depends on the refusal being monetisable, and what should a team do when it is not? Third: Setubandh's rate was wrong for two quarters because the measurement was wrong. What would have to be true of your own organisation for you to discover the same thing next month?

ThirteenGoing deeper

  1. What a large language model actually is. The claim that a fluent wrong answer is the same mechanism as a fluent right one only becomes convincing once you have seen the next-token objective; without it, every discussion here sounds like an excuse.
  2. Temperature and sampling. Explains why determinism is a testing tool rather than a truth tool, and gives you the vocabulary to refuse the most common proposed fix.
  3. Retrieval-augmented generation as an architecture. The decomposition in Table 2 is only usable if you know where retrieval can fail — chunking, embeddings, re-ranking, freshness — because each term in the equation has its own owner.
  4. Evals and what they actually measure. Everything in this page reduces to a measurement you either trust or do not; this is the topic that tells you which.
  5. Golden sets and LLM-as-judge. The Setubandh failure lives here. Judge-human agreement, stratification and re-measurement cadence are the specific skills.
  6. Guardrails and filtering. The engineering of span checks, entailment detectors and abstention rules, and the latency and precision costs each imposes.
  7. Red-teaming and adversarial testing. How the unanswerable tail gets found deliberately rather than by a customer's audit team.
  8. Tokens and tokenisation. Why arithmetic, spellings and rare proper nouns fail in characteristic ways, which explains a surprising share of "hallucinated" identifiers.
  9. The context window. Sets the ceiling on how much grounding you can supply, and introduces position effects that make long contexts less reliable than their size suggests.
  10. The transformer and attention. Enough architecture to reason about why more context can distract rather than help.
  11. Embeddings and vector search and similarity. The two topics that determine your P(miss) term, and the place where most retrieval failures actually originate.
  12. Inference versus training. Clarifies which of your levers are available at runtime and which require a training cycle — the distinction that decides whether a fix takes a week or a quarter.

Prashna Support Cloud, Vivran Health and Setubandh Freight Cloud are fictional companies. CDSCO, IRDAI and the DPDP Act are real Indian institutions and legislation, referenced only as market context; no real company or person is depicted.

Kathan Commerce Cloud: the assistant that knew the GST rate

Bengaluru, January 2026. A seller-support assistant has been confidently wrong about tax, and a product director has eight days to decide what to do before the Republic Day sale.

OneThe opening

On the morning of Thursday, 1 January 2026, Ananya Deshpande printed a single page and carried it into a meeting room on the second floor of Kathan Commerce Cloud's office in Koramangala, Bengaluru. The page had one paragraph on it, copied verbatim from a conversation log dated 11 December:

"Yes — the GST rate applicable to this category has been revised to 5% with effect from 1 December 2025 under the latest notification. You may file your December returns at the revised rate. Please retain the invoice-level HSN mapping for your records."

No such revision had occurred. The rate for that category had not moved. The sentence was fluent, correctly formatted, phrased exactly as a tax consultant would phrase it, and had been shown to 217 sellers who asked a version of the same question over eleven days. By the time a seller in Surat raised a support ticket on 22 December, some of them had already filed.

Ananya was Director of Product at Kathan and owned Sahayak, the AI assistant embedded in the company's seller-operations platform. She had until Friday, 9 January, to give the executive team a written recommendation. The Republic Day sale window — the first big commercial event of the calendar year across Flipkart, Amazon India, Meesho and the ONDC network storefronts — opened on 17 January, and Sahayak's question volume during such windows roughly tripled. Separately, Kathan's largest overseas account was due for renewal on 15 February and had asked, in writing, for an accuracy guarantee.

TwoCompany background

Kathan Commerce Cloud was founded in 2019 by two former category managers who had spent their twenties watching small sellers drown in marketplace operations. The company sold a seller-operations platform: catalogue management, inventory synchronisation across marketplaces, returns reconciliation, settlement tracking and payout dispute filing. By December 2025 it had 11,400 paying sellers, 220 employees, and annual recurring revenue of ₹58 crore. Plans ran from ₹1,499 a month for a single-marketplace seller to ₹24,999 a month for enterprise brands running six channels.

Its customers were the middle of the Indian e-commerce market: kitchenware brands in Moradabad, apparel labels in Tiruppur, phone-accessory sellers competing with boAt and Noise on price, and a growing set of D2C brands using Razorpay for their own storefronts alongside marketplace listings. Kathan's competitors were the tooling arms of larger logistics and payments players, and the free dashboards the marketplaces themselves provided. Its differentiation had always been that it answered the question a seller actually had at 11 p.m. on a Saturday, which was rarely "show me a dashboard" and almost always "why has my payout not come, and what do I do about it".

Sahayak had launched in July 2025 for exactly that reason. It was a retrieval-grounded assistant: a search index over Kathan's own operating procedures, the public seller help documentation of the marketplaces Kathan integrated with, and a folder of GST notifications and e-invoicing circulars maintained by a compliance analyst. A question came in, the index returned the most relevant passages, and a language model wrote an answer. Adoption had been unusually good — 6,900 of the 11,400 sellers had used it at least once a month — and in the October board pack the ticket-deflection rate had been reported as 43%.

ThreeThe situation

The December incident had not been the first sign. Nikita Grewal, Kathan's data scientist in Toronto, had run a manual audit in November: 600 answers sampled across the quarter, each read by two operations analysts in Bengaluru who marked whether every factual statement in the answer could be traced to a specific passage in the index. Her results are Exhibit 1. The headline figure was a 3.5% rate of unsupported statements, which the leadership team had received in a Monday review and filed away as acceptable.

What the headline hid was the distribution. Questions about settlement timelines and catalogue errors — the majority of volume, and the questions the index answered well — had rates near 1%. Questions about marketplace policy and, above all, about tax and compliance had rates five to nine times higher. Those were also the questions where a wrong answer cost a seller money.

Farhan Qureshi, the engineering lead in Pune, had a fix within two days of the ticket. He set the model's temperature to zero, added 240 words to the system prompt instructing it never to state a tax rate that did not appear verbatim in the retrieved text, and re-ran the eleven failing questions. All eleven now answered correctly. He posted the results at 1:15 a.m. India time with the message: "Fixed. Can we un-panic?"

Ritika Nair, who ran customer success from Singapore and covered the Gulf and Southeast Asian accounts, replied nine hours later, at the start of her day: "Farhan, it answered those eleven correctly. What is the rate on the eleven thousand questions we have not looked at? I have a client in Dubai asking me for a number and I do not have one."

That exchange framed the disagreement Ananya had to resolve. Farhan believed the December event was a defect, now patched. Ritika believed it was a property of the system that had merely become visible. Nikita's view, expressed carefully in a document nobody had fully read, was that the assistant had done nothing unusual on 11 December: the compliance folder contained no notification covering that category, the index had returned three loosely related circulars, and the model had produced the most plausible continuation available to it. It had not malfunctioned. It had filled a gap, in the register of a person who knew the answer.

FourThe people

Ananya Deshpande, Director of Product, Bengaluru. Six years at Kathan, three of them running the seller-operations product. She had championed Sahayak internally against a cautious CFO and knew that the October deflection number had been hers to quote. She wanted to be right rather than vindicated, which was harder than it sounded in the week of a board update.

Farhan Qureshi, Engineering Lead, Pune. Twelve engineers, a reputation for shipping through festive load without an outage, and a genuine conviction that the problem was a prompt problem. He also had a roadmap commitment — bulk catalogue repair — that would slip by a quarter if his team was pulled onto verification work.

Ritika Nair, Head of Customer Success, Singapore. She carried the renewals for 47 accounts across Singapore, Dubai and Colombo, including the India-export operations of Al Muheet Group's retail arm, worth ₹2.1 crore a year across 340 seller accounts. Al Muheet's procurement team had asked for a written accuracy commitment before the 15 February renewal. Ritika's honest position was that she would rather sell a narrower product she could describe accurately than a broad one she could not.

Sandeep Menon, Head of Sales, Edison, New Jersey. He sold to India-focused e-commerce operations run out of the United States and the Gulf, and Sahayak was, in his words, "the only thing in the deck that makes us look like 2026". He wanted the assistant on for the Republic Day window, on the reasonable ground that switching it off in the busiest fortnight of the quarter would be noticed by every customer and every competitor.

FiveExhibits

Exhibit 1 is the document the leadership team had already seen and misread. Read as a single number, 3.5% sounds like a system that is right 96.5% of the time. Read by row, it says something quite different: the assistant is excellent at the questions Kathan has documented properly and unreliable exactly where the documentation is thin. Applying the rates to volume, the quarter contained roughly 6,650 answers with an unsupported statement in them, of which about 2,858 were in the tax category — the smallest slice of volume and the largest slice of harm.

Whatever else Kathan did, it had no mechanism that made the system quieter where it was weaker.

SixThe options

Option A — patch and proceed. Keep Sahayak fully on for the Republic Day window with Farhan's temperature and prompt changes, plus a disclaimer line under every tax answer advising sellers to confirm with their chartered accountant. Cost: three engineer-days. Upside: no disruption before the sale, nothing to explain to customers, roadmap intact. Cost in risk: the November audit measured a system that already had a careful prompt; there is no evidence, and no measurement planned, that the new prompt changes the rate on the 30,400 tax questions a quarter. A disclaimer transfers no risk if the seller has already filed.

Option B — narrow the scope and verify what remains. Restrict Sahayak to the two categories the index covers properly — settlement and catalogue — plus marketplace policy questions where a verbatim passage exists. Add a mechanical check that every quoted figure appears exactly in a retrieved passage, and refuse all tax and compliance questions with a routed handoff to Kathan's compliance desk. Cost: ticket deflection falls from 43% to an estimated 29%, requiring about nine additional support agents at ₹43.2 lakh a year, and roughly ₹18 lakh of engineering over three weeks for the span check and routing. Upside: the residual risk sits in categories where a wrong answer costs a follow-up rather than a filing, and Ritika gets a number and a scope she can put in front of Al Muheet.

Option C — withdraw and rebuild. Switch Sahayak off, build a stratified golden set with the compliance analyst and two senior ops staff, add a verification layer and index-freshness tooling, and relaunch in April. Cost: ₹62 lakh of engineering, an estimated ₹1.4 crore of churn, and a visible retreat during the busiest fortnight of the quarter. Upside: Kathan relaunches with measurement it can defend, and never has to explain a second incident.

SevenQuestions for discussion

  1. What exactly happened on 11 December? Describe the failure in mechanical terms, without using the word "bug", and say what the system would have had to be built differently to avoid it.
  2. Exhibit 1 reports a 3.5% rate and the leadership team accepted it. What is wrong with that number as a decision input, and what number should Ananya have asked for instead?
  3. Farhan's patch made eleven failing questions pass. What would you need to see before you accepted that as evidence of improvement, and how cheaply could Kathan produce it before 9 January?
  4. Which option should Ananya recommend, and what precisely should Ritika be authorised to put in writing to Al Muheet Group before 15 February?

EightA note for the learner

The lens for this case is the distinction between a hallucination and a confabulation. A language model does not look up facts and occasionally retrieve the wrong one. It produces the most likely continuation of the text in front of it, and when the retrieved passages contain nothing that answers the question, the most likely continuation is a well-formed sentence of the kind that usually answers such questions — a rate, a date, a notification reference. Nothing malfunctioned on 11 December. The system did exactly what it does when it is right. That is why the answer read like a tax consultant's answer, and that is why 217 sellers acted on it.

Two consequences follow, and they are the whole of the analysis. First, the rate can be reduced by changing the input — grounding the answer in documents that actually contain it — and by verifying the output, but it cannot be argued down by instruction. Farhan's prompt is not worthless; instructions do shift the model's behaviour. But eleven questions passing is not a measurement, and a prompt cannot manufacture a fact the index does not hold. Second, because the residue is permanent, the design question is not "how do we eliminate this" but "where are we willing to place it". Exhibit 1 answers that question uncomfortably: Kathan has placed its residue in the tax category, where a wrong answer costs a seller real money and where Kathan holds the least documentation.

A well-reasoned answer will therefore stop treating the rate as a single quantity to be minimised and start treating it as a distribution to be moved. It will also notice Exhibit 3: the assistant's refusal rate is flat while its reliability varies tenfold, which means the product has no way of being quieter where it is weaker. That, rather than the prompt, is the design defect.

One defensible path. Ananya recommends Option B, with three specifics. Sahayak stays live through the Republic Day window — withdrawing a working feature during peak demand imposes a certain ₹1.4 crore of estimated churn to avoid an uncertain risk — but with tax and compliance questions hard-refused and routed to the compliance desk from 12 January, before volume triples. Every quoted figure in a remaining answer is mechanically checked against the retrieved passage before display, which is three weeks of work and removes the class of error where the assistant quotes something that does not exist. And Ritika is authorised to give Al Muheet Group a scope statement rather than a guarantee: a written list of the question types Sahayak will answer, the audited unsupported rate for each with the sample size, the refusal behaviour outside that scope, and a commitment to a joint quarterly audit. The reasoning is that a narrower promise Kathan can keep is worth more at renewal than a broader one it cannot, and that the ₹43.2 lakh of additional support cost is the honest price of the coverage the product was quietly claiming for free.

What makes this defensible rather than correct is that it accepts a real loss. Deflection falls by fourteen points, Sandeep's deck gets weaker, and the roadmap slips. A reasonable person could argue for Option C on the ground that Kathan has now had one incident and cannot afford a second in a compliance-adjacent product. What is not defensible is Option A, because it responds to a property of the technology with a change of wording, and then measures nothing.

Kathan Commerce Cloud and Al Muheet Group are fictional. Flipkart, Amazon India, Meesho, ONDC, Razorpay, boAt and Noise are real firms and networks named only as market context; no real company or person is depicted as having done anything improper.

Pralekh Legal Cloud: the number on the questionnaire

Bengaluru, the night of Sunday 8 March 2026. A contract-review company has discovered that the accuracy figure it has been quoting for five months was measured by a method that could not have detected the thing it was measuring.

OneSunday night, Indiranagar

Ishaan Vaidya had three documents open and no intention of closing any of them. It was a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 8 March 2026, the Holi long weekend had emptied the office, and the executive meeting was at nine the next morning.

The first document was a vendor security and diligence questionnaire from a large private-sector bank, question 41 of which read: "State the measured rate of factually unsupported output for any generative component, the method of measurement, and the date of last measurement." The answer field, filled in by Pralekh's sales head on 27 February, read: "Less than 1% (internal evaluation, January 2026)." The response was due back, signed, on 13 March.

The second was a five-page memorandum from Dr Amrita Sen in Toronto, dated Thursday 5 March, explaining that the January evaluation had been scored by a language model which had been instructed to check "whether the answer is consistent with the source contract" and which, on inspection, had been marking an answer as supported whenever the clause number it cited existed somewhere in the document. Whether the quoted text of that clause bore any relation to what the answer said had never been checked. On a re-scored sample, the rate was 4.3%. On questions about schedules and annexures it was 9.1%.

The third was an email from the general counsel of Rasikh Contracting LLC in Dubai, whose renewal was due on 31 March and worth ₹3.6 crore, asking politely whether Pralekh had, as promised in December, "completed the remediation".

Ishaan was Vice President of Product. He had joined Pralekh Legal Cloud in 2022, before there was a generative layer to worry about, and he had been the person who wrote the launch note for Ask Pralekh in August 2025. By Thursday 12 March he had to say something to a board that had approved a growth plan built on that launch.

TwoCompany history, and the decision that still binds

Pralekh Legal Cloud was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by Meghna Rau, a former in-house counsel at a large engineering conglomerate, and Suresh Iyengar, who had run search infrastructure at an e-commerce company. The original product was unglamorous and good: contract extraction. Upload ten thousand supply agreements, and Pralekh would identify the parties, the term, the renewal mechanism, the payment terms, the indemnity, the limitation of liability, the governing law and the dispute-resolution clause, and put them in a table you could query.

The extraction worked because of a decision taken in 2023 that the company has never been able to revisit. To get accuracy high enough to sell to listed companies, Pralekh built a proprietary clause taxonomy — 214 clause types — and had a team of eighteen paralegals in Coimbatore hand-label 40,000 clauses against it. The index was then built with the clause as the unit: each indexed chunk was one clause, cleanly bounded, tagged with its taxonomy type. It gave Pralekh an accuracy story its competitors could not match in 2023, and it won the company its first ₹1 crore accounts.

The taxonomy covered the body of a contract. It did not cover schedules, annexures, rate cards, side letters or amendment letters, because in 2023 nobody was asking questions about those. Everything downstream — the extraction tables, the reporting, the customer-facing clause library, and, from 2025, the retrieval index behind the generative assistant — was keyed to that taxonomy. Roughly 900 customers' historical extractions were tied to it. Re-indexing the corpus on a different unit had been costed twice: ₹2.8 crore and about five months, with a migration that would invalidate saved queries and dashboards across the customer base.

Ask Pralekh, launched on 14 August 2025, was a generative layer bolted on to that index. A user typed a question in English — does this agreement let the counterparty assign without our consent? — the index returned the most relevant clauses, and a language model wrote a paragraph. It was the fastest-adopted feature in the company's history. It was also, structurally, a system that could only ground its answers in the parts of a contract the 2023 taxonomy had thought worth indexing.

ThreeThe industry around it

Indian enterprise legal technology in 2026 was a real market with real buyers. In-house legal teams at listed manufacturers, banks and IT services firms had budgets, and the compliance load kept growing: the DPDP Act's data-processing agreement requirements had forced a wave of contract amendments through 2025; SEBI's listing obligations required listed entities to identify and disclose material contracts and related-party arrangements on a timetable; the MSMED Act's forty-five-day payment rule had made payment-term extraction a board-level question for anyone with a long supplier tail. Every one of those obligations turned on what a contract actually said.

Pralekh competed with domestic contract-lifecycle players, with the legal modules that large Indian SaaS companies such as Zoho and Freshworks had made buyers comfortable buying from Indian vendors, and — increasingly — with the system integrators. Infosys and TCS both offered contract-analysis services wrapped around third-party models, and their presence had reset what buyers expected to pay.

Pralekh's exposure was not only domestic. About 31% of revenue came from outside India: construction and trading groups in the Gulf, and the India-facing legal operations of a few US firms handled by Gautam Trivedi's team in New Jersey. Rasikh Contracting LLC in Dubai was the largest of these, using Pralekh across roughly 14,000 subcontracts governed by UAE law and a mix of FIDIC forms. The DPDP Act constrained what Pralekh could do about any of it: customer contracts contained personal data, and Pralekh's own data-processing agreements with several Indian customers restricted processing to infrastructure in India. That closed off the simplest engineering response — routing difficult questions to a larger model hosted abroad — without a round of customer consents that would itself take a quarter.

FourThe situation, in sequence

14 August 2025. Ask Pralekh launches to all customers. Internal testing had been done by the Pune team on 180 questions written by two engineers.

9 October 2025. Amrita Sen's team in Toronto stands up the first proper evaluation: 2,000 questions sampled from production logs, scored by a language model acting as judge. Result: 1.4% of answers contain an unsupported assertion. The number goes into the October board pack and into the sales deck. What was believed: that the system was already good enough. What is now known: the judge prompt asked whether the answer was "consistent with the source contract", and the judge treated the existence of a cited clause number as sufficient evidence of consistency.

3 December 2025. Nadir Al Owais, general counsel at Rasikh Contracting, runs an unannounced test with two of his associates: 120 questions across 40 subcontracts. Fourteen answers — 11.7% — refer to a clause whose text does not say what the answer claims. Nine of the fourteen concern payment milestones, which in FIDIC-form subcontracts live in the schedules. Rasikh's finding is emailed to Shalini Prabhu in Singapore with a request for remediation by the end of the quarter. What was believed inside Pralekh: that 11.7% and 1.4% could not both be right, and that Rasikh's associates had probably been marking stylistic imprecision as error. Nobody reconciled the two measurements.

19 January 2026. Pune ships "citation mode": every assertion in an answer carries an inline reference, and hovering reveals the clause text. The October evaluation is re-run with the same judge. Result: 0.6%. The improvement is attributed to citation mode and reported to customers as "a fifty-seven per cent reduction in unsupported output". What is now known: the judge could not have detected the difference, because the judge had never been reading the clause text.

11 February 2026. Bhargav Alloys Ltd, a listed manufacturer in Pune and a Pralekh customer since 2021, uses Ask Pralekh during a diligence exercise on a bolt-on acquisition. Two errors surface a week later. In one supply agreement, the assistant reports a change-of-control clause requiring counterparty consent; the agreement contains no such clause, and the assistant's citation points to a clause about assignment of receivables. In a second agreement, the assistant reports no change-of-control restriction; the restriction exists, in Schedule 4. The diligence timetable slips by eleven days. Bhargav Alloys invokes the accuracy warranty in its master services agreement and opens a thirty-day cure period that ends on 18 March.

27 February 2026. Gautam Trivedi completes the bank's diligence questionnaire. He asks Suresh Iyengar on a call for "the accuracy number", is told "under one per cent, January", and writes it in.

3–5 March 2026. Amrita, investigating the Bhargav Alloys errors, reads the judge prompt for the first time. She hand-labels 300 answers drawn from the same production logs, using a stricter definition: an assertion is supported only if the cited clause text, read plainly, states it. Overall rate 4.3%; on questions whose true answer lies in a schedule or annexure, 9.1%. She writes the memorandum on Ishaan's screen.

6 March 2026. Johanna Pfeiffer in Berlin circulates user research conducted after citation mode shipped. Self-reported trust in the assistant's answers rose twelve points. The proportion of sessions in which a user opened the underlying contract document fell from 38% to 19%.

FiveThe people

Ishaan Vaidya, VP Product, Bengaluru. Wrote the launch note, owns the roadmap, and has to speak on Thursday. Position: the company must correct the record before it signs anything else. Incentive: his credibility is tied to Ask Pralekh's adoption numbers, which are genuinely excellent. Not saying: he read Rasikh's December test results, thought the discrepancy was strange, and moved on because January's roadmap was already committed.

Meghna Rau, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Position: fix it quietly, fast, and do not turn a measurement error into a disclosure event. Incentive: a secondary share sale is being negotiated with two existing investors at a valuation that rests substantially on the AI layer's adoption. Not saying: the term sheet has a representation about the accuracy of information provided during diligence.

Suresh Iyengar, co-founder and Head of Engineering, Pune. Position: the real problem is the 2023 index unit; approve the ₹2.8 crore re-index and the schedule questions stop failing. Incentive: he has wanted to rebuild that index for two years. Not saying: his team wrote the judge prompt, and he approved it in a fifteen-minute review.

Incentive: she found the error and is right about it. Not saying: her own re-score is 300 answers labelled by one person — herself — and she has not measured inter-labeller agreement on it.

Incentive: she proposed exactly this in July 2025 and was overruled. Not saying: her post-launch study has twenty-four participants, none of them from the Gulf accounts.

Incentive: her retention number is the one that will move. "Nadir asked me in January what our rate was and I told him what I had been told. I now have to go back to him three weeks before renewal. I would like to know what I am allowed to say before I get on that call, not after."Shalini Prabhu, chat thread, 6 March, 07:12 SGT
"If we amend question 41, their risk team re-opens the whole file and we are out of the cycle until the next budget year. That is ₹9 crore. I filled it in with a number an engineering co-founder gave me on a call. I do not think the issue is the questionnaire."Gautam Trivedi, call notes, 7 March
"My concern is narrow and I will keep saying it. We have made a written statement of measured fact to a regulated financial institution, in a diligence process, which we now have reason to believe was wrong. Whatever else we decide, that sentence has to be dealt with on its own terms."Farida Merchant, note to Ishaan, 7 March
"Everyone is arguing about the rate. Nobody is arguing about the fact that we have made lawyers half as likely to open the contract. If the answers were perfect that would be a triumph. They are not perfect, and we have removed the person who would have caught them."Johanna Pfeiffer, design review, 6 March

EightThe options as Ishaan sees them

Correct the record. Amend the questionnaire response before 13 March with the re-scored figure, its method and its sample size; write to Rasikh, Bhargav Alloys and the eleven other accounts that were sent the January number; tell the board on Thursday. The cost is the bank pipeline, probably the Rasikh renewal, and a conversation with investors in the middle of a secondary. The benefit is that nothing worse accumulates.

Measure properly, then speak. Commission the ₹38 lakh re-measurement with three labellers and a published rubric; ask the bank for a two-week extension on question 41; tell nobody else until there is a number worth standing behind. The cost is a fortnight of silence during which the assistant continues to answer 206,000 questions a month, and the possibility that the extension request itself raises the question Gautam is trying to avoid.

Change the product, not the number. Take Johanna's July 2025 proposal off the shelf: stop generating prose, and have Ask Pralekh return the retrieved clauses with the relevant passage highlighted and a one-line navigational summary that makes no assertion. The cost is the feature's differentiation and most of the adoption story in the board pack. The benefit is that the failure mode largely disappears, because the product stops making claims.

Ishaan had written all three on a single page and had been staring at the page for an hour. What bothered him was not that the options were hard. It was that all three of them accepted the same framing — that the company had a number which was wrong and needed to be made right — and he was no longer sure that was the shape of the problem. Amrita's 4.3% was itself one person's labels on 300 answers with an unmatched sample. Rasikh's 11.7% came from contracts chosen because they were in dispute. Exhibit 5 said complaints were falling and Exhibit 4 suggested that was exactly what one would expect from a product that had made its users stop checking. Somewhere underneath all of it was a question nobody at Pralekh had written down: what was a lawyer supposed to do with an answer from Ask Pralekh, and had anyone ever designed for that?

NineThe deadline and the hard constraints

The executive meeting is at 09:00 on Monday 9 March. The board meets on Thursday 12 March. The bank's questionnaire is due signed on 13 March. Bhargav Alloys' thirty-day cure period ends on 18 March, and Farida's reading is that a cure requires a demonstrated remediation, not a plan for one. Rasikh Contracting's ₹3.6 crore renewal falls on 31 March, and Nadir Al Owais has asked a direct question that Shalini cannot answer without a decision.

Money and people constrain the rest. Runway is fourteen months and hiring has been frozen since November, so the re-index and the re-measurement compete for the same eight engineers and two analysts. The DPDP Act and Pralekh's own data-processing agreements prevent routing customer contracts to any model hosted outside India without fresh consents from at least forty customers, which closes the option of simply using a better model for schedule questions. The 2023 taxonomy cannot be replaced without invalidating saved queries for roughly 900 customers, several of whom use those queries for SEBI disclosure workflows on a statutory timetable. And the master services agreement with Bhargav Alloys contains the only accuracy warranty Pralekh has ever signed, which Meghna approved personally in 2021 because the customer was the company's first listed logo.

TenQuestions for discussion

  1. Describe mechanically what happened when Ask Pralekh reported a change-of-control clause that did not exist and missed one that did. Are these two errors the same kind of event or different kinds, and does the distinction matter to what Pralekh should do?
  2. Exhibit 1, Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 5 point in different directions. For each, state what it measures, what it cannot measure, and what you would need before you would put it in front of a board.
  3. Citation mode improved the measured rate and, on Exhibit 4's evidence, reduced the behaviour that catches errors. Was shipping it a good decision, a bad one, or a decision that cannot be evaluated on the evidence available?
  4. Suresh argues the index is the problem and the re-index is the fix. Suppose the re-index were free and instantaneous. What would Pralekh's rate be afterwards, and what is the basis for your estimate?
  5. Whose incentives in Section Five are most likely to distort the Monday meeting, and what could Ishaan change about how that meeting is run — agenda, attendance, what is circulated beforehand — to reduce that distortion without accusing anyone of anything?
  6. What should Ishaan do on Monday morning, in what order, and with what specifically said to whom? What should he tell the board on Thursday — and if a director asks him whether Pralekh can guarantee that this will not happen again, what is his answer?

ElevenSunday, later

At twenty past one, Ishaan closed the questionnaire and opened the Bhargav Alloys transcript again. The answer about the change-of-control clause was four sentences long. It was well organised. It cited Clause 19.2, which existed. It read exactly like the answers that were right — the same careful tone, the same structure, the same confidence — and he understood, sitting there, that this was not a coincidence but the whole of the matter: the system had not done anything different on 11 February from what it did on the thousands of occasions it was useful.

He thought about writing to Amrita and asking how long a proper measurement would take if she had three labellers instead of one, and then thought about what he would say to Shalini if the answer was five weeks. He thought about Johanna's twenty-four lawyers, half as likely to open a contract they were being paid to read. He thought about the ₹2.8 crore, and the eight engineers who could not do two things at once, and the sentence in question 41 that was sitting, signed and unsigned, in a folder on a bank's server.

Outside, somebody was still setting off leftover Holi crackers on 12th Main. The meeting was in less than eight hours. Ishaan opened a blank document, typed the words What we know, what we believe, and how we know the difference, and then sat looking at them for a long time without adding anything else.

Pralekh Legal Cloud, Rasikh Contracting LLC and Bhargav Alloys Ltd are fictional companies, as are all individuals named. Zoho, Freshworks, Infosys and TCS, and the DPDP Act, the SEBI listing obligations and the MSMED Act, appear only as real market and regulatory context; no real company or person is depicted as having done anything improper.

Hallucination and confabulation

Is this a bug they will eventually fix, or a property we have to design around forever? A working explainer built around one decision at one company.

Section onePune, 14 October 2025

Meera Raghunathan had eleven working days and one uncomfortable sentence to write. She was Vice President of Product at Dastavez Systems, a 140-person company in Baner, Pune, that sold a document-grounded assistant to Indian insurers, banks and hospital chains. The product did one thing: it read a customer's own documents — policy wordings, circulars, standard operating procedures — and answered questions about them in plain English and Hindi. The pilot that mattered was with a large Indian general insurer, forty claims assessors across Nagpur, Indore and Kochi, and a contract worth ₹3.2 crore a year if it converted from pilot to production.

On 3 October, an assessor in Nagpur had asked the assistant whether water damage to a basement godown was payable under a commercial property policy. The assistant replied in three sentences. The second sentence read: "Clause 4(b) of the policy excludes damage caused by hydrostatic pressure to below-ground structures." The clause number was in bold. The wording was in quotation marks. The assessor repudiated a claim of ₹6.4 lakh and moved on to the next file.

There was no Clause 4(b) about hydrostatic pressure. The policy's Clause 4 ran from (a) to (e) and covered wear and tear, wilful act, consequential loss, war and nuclear risk. The sentence the assistant produced was not in the customer's document at all. It was, however, an entirely ordinary sentence — the sort of exclusion that appears in property wordings the world over, phrased exactly as an underwriter would phrase it. The customer complained, the insurer's grievance cell reversed the repudiation within eleven days as IRDAI timelines require, and the insurer's compliance head sent Meera a two-line email: can you guarantee this will not happen again?

Vikram Bhatia, Meera's engineering lead in Bengaluru, had an answer ready by the next standup. Set the temperature to zero, he said, and add a line to the system prompt: never state anything that is not in the retrieved documents. He had already tried it on the failing question and the assistant now answered correctly. Meera's instinct was that this was true and useless at the same time. Her real question, the one she had to resolve before Friday, was not how to fix that answer. It was whether she was looking at a defect that would be patched out of existence in the next model release, or at a permanent property of the technology that her product, her contract and her customer's claims process would have to be built around.

Section twoThe idea, and the better word for it

A hallucination, in the language that has settled around large language models since 2022, is content that a model states with the same fluency and confidence as everything else it says, but which has no support either in the input it was given or in the world. Two words in that definition do the work. Support means a specific, checkable basis: a span of text in a supplied document, or a fact that is true. Confidence means the surface style of the output — the bold clause number, the quotation marks — which is a property of the prose, not a measurement of anything.

The word itself arrived by an odd route. In machine learning it was used through the late 2010s for image-captioning systems that described objects not present in the photograph, and for neural machine translation systems that emitted fluent target-language sentences unrelated to the source. It escaped into general use after 2022, when conversational models put the behaviour in front of hundreds of millions of people. Almost immediately a group of researchers and clinicians objected to it, and their objection is the single most useful thing a product manager can learn about the topic.

Confabulation is the term they prefer, borrowed from clinical neuropsychology, where it describes patients — classically those with Korsakoff's syndrome, first characterised by the Russian physician Sergei Korsakoff in the 1880s — who fill gaps in memory with coherent, plausible, sincerely offered narrative. The confabulating patient is not lying and is not aware of any gap. Hallucination implies a perceptual system misfiring: something was there to be seen, and the machinery saw it wrongly. That is not what happens here. Nothing misfires. The model produces a likely continuation of the text so far, which is exactly what it was built to do and exactly what it does when it is right.

The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "The system is not reporting what it knows; it is producing the most likely next piece of text. A likely continuation is usually true and sometimes false, and it looks identical either way — so we lower the rate with grounding and verification, and we design the workflow for what is left."

That framing answers the question the topic exists to answer. If confabulation were a bug — a fault in an otherwise sound mechanism — then waiting for the next model would be a rational strategy. Because it is a property of the mechanism, waiting is not a strategy. Better models measurably reduce the rate; several benchmarks show large drops between model generations on the same questions. None of them drives it to zero, and none of them can, because a system that produces likely continuations will, on the questions where the true answer is unlikely text, produce likely false text instead.

Section threeHow it actually works, step by step

Start with what the model is. A large language model is a function that takes a sequence of tokens — word fragments, roughly three-quarters of a word each — and returns a probability distribution over which token comes next. It was trained by being shown enormous quantities of human text and adjusted until the text it predicted matched the text that actually followed. The objective was likelihood, not truth. No stage of that process asked whether a sentence was accurate; it asked whether the sentence was the kind of thing that gets written.

Generation then proceeds one token at a time. Sampling is the act of choosing a token from that distribution; temperature is a dial that flattens or sharpens the distribution before choosing. At high temperature the model picks unlikely tokens more often and the prose becomes surprising; at temperature zero it always takes the most probable token. Vikram's instinct was that unpredictability was the enemy, and therefore that removing unpredictability would remove the error. Figure 1 shows why that reasoning fails. In the Nagpur case the invented exclusion was not an unlikely token that slipped through — it was the most likely continuation, because that is how property exclusions are written.

Grounding changes the input rather than the mechanism. In retrieval-augmented generation, the architecture Dastavez already used, the question is first converted into a search query, a search engine over the customer's own documents returns the most relevant chunks of text, and those chunks are pasted into the prompt above the question. The model now has the real Clause 4 in front of it, and the real clause is now a very likely thing to copy. The rate falls, often by a factor of three or four. What has not changed is what happens when retrieval brings back nothing useful. The model is still obliged to produce a continuation, and "I cannot find this" remains a low-probability sentence unless the model has been specifically trained and instructed to prefer it.

Four steps in that pipeline are routinely left implicit, and each of them was live at Dastavez. First, retrieval is a search problem with its own failure rate; the Nagpur policy was a scanned PDF whose clause table had been split across two chunks. Second, refusal has to be earned: abstention competes with fluency, and a model that abstains too readily is useless. Third, the confidence in the output is a learned style, copied from the confident documents in the training corpus, and carries no information about correctness. Fourth — the one that caught Dastavez hardest — citations are generated text too. A clause number in an answer is just more tokens unless something in the system actually goes and checks that the cited span exists.

Section fourA worked example, with the arithmetic shown

Meera did the calculation herself on a Wednesday evening, because she wanted a number to put in front of the compliance head rather than an adjective. Forty assessors, twenty-two working days a month, an average of eighteen questions each per working day: 40 × 22 × 18 = 15,840 questions a month. On a golden set of 500 questions written by two of the insurer's senior assessors and labelled by hand, Dastavez had measured an unsupported-statement rate of 8.2% for the model answering with no documents at all, and 2.1% for the same model with retrieval.
