+ retrieval over the customer's wordings2.1%333Real clauses become the likeliest thing to copy
+ verbatim span check on every citation0.80%126Rejects answers quoting text absent from the source
+ assessor catches it while reading0.24%38Human review, measured at 70% catch rate
Reaches a claims decision0.24%38Roughly two per assessor per year

Golden set n = 500, labelled independently by two senior assessors, disagreements adjudicated by a third. The 70% human catch rate comes from a shadow study of 220 answers in September 2025 and is the softest number in the table.

The span check is worth explaining because it is the cheapest engineering in the list. Every time the assistant puts text in quotation marks and attaches a clause reference, a small deterministic program searches the retrieved chunks for that exact string. If the string is not there, the answer is blocked and rewritten. That single mechanism took the residue from 333 to 126 a month — a 62% reduction — and involved no model change at all. It is the clearest illustration of the principle that confabulation is managed by architecture and verification rather than by persuasion.

Now change one input. Vikram proposed raising the retrieval depth from the top 5 chunks to the top 20, on the theory that most failures were retrieval misses. Re-running the golden set, chunk-level recall rose from 88% to 96%, and the unsupported rate fell from 2.1% to 1.6% — 333 down to 253 a month, a real but modest gain. Two other things moved. The abstention rate fell from 6.4% to 4.1%, because with more text in front of it the model found something to say more often, which sounds good and is not: some of those new answers were grounded in the wrong document. And a new failure appeared that had not existed before: in 9 of the 500 questions the assistant answered correctly but from the 2023 version of the wording rather than the 2025 endorsement, because both were now in the context window and nothing told it which was current. Deeper retrieval reduced one failure and created another. That is the characteristic shape of work in this area.

Section fiveThe nuances a learner has to absorb

Support is a definition, not a fact of nature

Before any rate can be measured, somebody must decide what counts as support. Is a paraphrase of the retrieved clause supported? Is a correct inference drawn from two clauses supported? Dastavez's first eval marked inference as unsupported and produced a frightening 14% rate; the second marked it as supported and produced 2.1%. Neither number was wrong. When a team quotes a hallucination rate, the first question is what their labellers were told.

Groundedness and correctness are different measurements

An answer can be perfectly faithful to a retrieved document and still be false, because the document is out of date — this is exactly the 2023-wording failure above. Conversely an answer can be true about the world and unsupported by the supplied documents, which a faithfulness eval will mark as a hallucination. Teams argue for weeks without noticing that one person is measuring faithfulness and the other accuracy.

Temperature zero buys reproducibility, not truth

Determinism is genuinely valuable: it makes evals stable and bug reports reproducible. But as Figure 1 shows, if the modal continuation is wrong, greedy decoding produces the wrong answer every time rather than sometimes. In several tasks it also degrades quality by removing useful diversity.

Prompting moves the rate; it never removes the mechanism

Instructions such as "answer only from the provided context" and "say you don't know if the answer is absent" do work — they shift probability mass toward abstention, sometimes substantially. They saturate quickly. A 900-word system prompt full of prohibitions is a common sight in companies that have mistaken a design problem for a wording problem.

Every reduction is bought with refusals

This is the discipline that separates people who understand the topic from people who use the word. Figure 2's curve is the object under management. The product question is never "how do we get to zero" but "at what abstention rate does this stop being useful to a claims assessor working through eighteen files a day".

The model's own confidence is not evidence

Asking "are you sure?" produces another generation, subject to the same mechanism, and models frequently reverse a correct answer under mild pressure. There are weak but real signals — the token-level probabilities the model assigns to its own output, and self-consistency, where the same question is asked five times and disagreement is treated as a warning — but neither is a confidence score in the sense a risk committee would recognise.

Retrieval relocates the failure

Grounding converts a generation problem into a search problem, and search has its own pathologies: missed chunks, split tables, stale indexes, near-duplicate documents from different years. Dastavez's most dangerous residual failure after all the fixes was not invention at all — it was confident, well-cited, correctly-quoted answers from a superseded policy version.

An aggregate rate hides the distribution that matters

A 2.1% average across a golden set may be 0.3% on the routine four-fifths of questions and 20% on the unusual tail — and the tail is where the ₹6.4 lakh decisions live. Severity is equally uneven: an invented clause number that repudiates a claim and an invented phone number in a summary are not the same event. Any serious measurement is stratified by question type and weighted by consequence.

Section sixHow this differs across product types and company stages

In consumer products the tolerance is comparatively high and the mitigation is mostly interface design: recipes, itineraries and general explanations are checked by the user against reality within minutes, and the cost of a wrong sentence is annoyance. The failure that hurts consumer products is not the average rate but the screenshot — one confidently invented statement in a sensitive category, shared widely. The design response is scope: refuse whole categories rather than trying to be accurate in them.

In B2B, which is Dastavez's world, the person reading the answer is accountable for acting on it, and the product is bought by someone who will be asked about it by a regulator. Here the mitigation is evidentiary: span-verified citations, visible source documents, an audit trail of what the assistant said and what the human did next. The contract language matters too — Meera's commercial instinct was that promising zero would be both false and, once written into a service agreement, catastrophic.

In marketplaces and other multi-sided products the confabulation is often about the other side of the market: an assistant that invents a seller's return policy, a delivery window or a fee. The injured party is not the user who asked, and therefore never reports the error; the feedback loop that would normally surface the problem is missing. Marketplaces need active sampling rather than passive complaints.

Stage changes the answer as much as product type. An early-stage company can and should narrow scope aggressively — answer four question types extremely well, refuse everything else — because it has no brand to spend and no compliance function to satisfy. A large company usually cannot narrow scope, because the assistant was sold as general, so it invests instead in measurement infrastructure, severity classification and the workflow controls that ensure no consequential decision rests on a single generated sentence.

Section sevenCommon mistakes and the cheapest diagnostic for each

Treating it as a prompt bug. The symptom is visible from outside: a system prompt that has grown to hundreds of words of prohibitions, and a team that responds to each incident by adding another sentence. The underlying misunderstanding is that the model is disobeying. The cheapest diagnostic is an A/B run of the old and new prompt over a fixed 200-question adversarial set, which almost always shows a small, non-zero, deeply unimpressive improvement.

Measuring only on answerable questions. The symptom is an eval scoring 97% while support tickets accumulate. The misunderstanding is that a golden set written by the team represents what users ask. The diagnostic costs an afternoon: pull 100 real production questions, have a domain expert label how many are answerable from the corpus at all, and re-measure separately on the answerable and unanswerable halves. The unanswerable half is where confabulation lives.

Trusting a citation because it is displayed. The symptom is users reporting that the citations "look right". The misunderstanding is that the citation was retrieved rather than written. The diagnostic is the verbatim span match described above — run it retrospectively over a month of logs and count how many quoted spans do not exist in the cited document. At Dastavez that number, before the fix, was 11%.

Buying or selling a guarantee. The symptom is a vendor claim of a hallucination-free system, or a sales deck promising one. The misunderstanding is the same one Meera started with: that this is a defect awaiting a patch. The diagnostic is one question — what is your abstention rate at that number, and how did you define support? — and the quality of the answer tells you everything about the seriousness of the team.

Section eightWhat good looks like

Handled well, this decision produces a small number of unglamorous artefacts. There is a stratified golden set, several hundred questions, built with the customer's own experts and including questions the corpus cannot answer. There is a published operating point: a stated unsupported rate, a stated abstention rate, and the date and version of the model and index at which both were measured. There is a verification layer that checks generated citations mechanically. There is a severity taxonomy that separates a mis-stated clause from a mis-stated phone number, and monitoring that reports the two separately. And there is a workflow change on the customer's side: no repudiation, no disbursement, no clinical instruction on the strength of an assistant's answer alone.

What is absent is equally diagnostic: no promise of zero, no reliance on prompt wording as the primary control, and no single headline number quoted without its companion.

Section nineWhat Meera decided

On Friday 17 October, Meera sent the compliance head a reply that did not contain the word guarantee. She wrote that unsupported statements were a property of the technology rather than a defect in the installation, that Dastavez would contract to a measured operating point rather than to zero, and that the pilot would resume on 1 November under four changes: citation spans verified mechanically before display, mandatory abstention on questions where two policy versions were both retrieved, a severity-weighted monthly report shared with the insurer's compliance team, and a written change to the claims SOP stating that no repudiation may rest on the assistant's output without the assessor opening the cited clause. She offered the insurer an exit at any point in the first two quarters if the reported rate exceeded 0.5% on consequential questions.

The insurer's board approved the production rollout on 24 October, and the compliance head told Meera afterwards that the reason was the exit clause: a vendor willing to be measured was more credible than one promising perfection. What to learn next follows directly from those four commitments. Evals and what they actually measure is the discipline behind the golden set and the reason an aggregate rate misleads. Golden sets and LLM-as-judge explains how to scale labelling when 500 hand-labelled questions stop being enough. Guardrails and filtering is the engineering of the span check and the abstention rules. Red-teaming and adversarial testing is how the unanswerable tail gets found before a customer finds it.

Two questions to sit with. First: for your product, what is the abstention rate at which the assistant stops being worth opening — and do you know that number, or have you only ever discussed the error rate? Second: if your system produced one confidently invented sentence tomorrow, which control in your product would catch it, and how long would it take you to notice that the control had failed?

Dastavez Systems is a fictional company. IRDAI is India's real insurance regulator; the regulatory timelines referenced are used only as market context and no real firm or person is described.
